articles.title: Nvidia shares drop after CEO Jensen Huang admits affair with suspected Chinese spy; what it means for company
articles.summary: Nvidia shares declined in after-hours trading on Monday following the announcement of an internal investigation to find out if the company’s chief
articles.body: Nvidia shares declined in after-hours trading on Monday following the announcement of an internal investigation to find out if the company’s chief executive Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The investigation has raised questions about Jensen Huang’s future at the AI chipmaker which is among the most valuable listed companies in the world.Announced on Sunday, the investigation has drawn attention to Huang's position at Nvidia, the world's most valuable chipmaker. His future is also under scrutiny because of his prominent role as one of the leading salesmen of the artificial intelligence boom.Jensen Huang, 63, has headed Nvidia since he established the company in 1993 alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. His long tenure makes him one of Silicon Valley's longest-serving chief executives among company founders.Born in Taiwan and brought up in the US, Huang emerged as a key figure in the artificial intelligence revolution. He steered Nvidia from its original business of manufacturing graphics chips for video games to becoming the world's leading supplier of AI processors.Jensen Huang & the 'Chinese spy' scandalThe company launched the internal inquiry following a media report alleging that Huang had a close association with a Chinese businesswoman who had allegedly shared information with Beijing. In a message to Nvidia employees, Huang acknowledged that he had been unfaithful to his wife but did not provide details about the relationship.The New York Times reported last month that Huang had been involved in a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is not related to him. US authorities investigated Alice Huang and concluded that she was an asset of Chinese intelligence.Megaspeed's website identifies the company as an Nvidia Cloud Partner in the Asia-Pacific region. It also lists Nvidia's GB200 NVL72 and HGX H100 chips among the products it offers.The developments also had repercussions in South Korea. Madison Huang, Jensen Huang's daughter and an Nvidia executive, called off a scheduled visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference due to begin on Monday, according to companies that had been due to meet her.Madison Huang had been scheduled to visit South Korean artificial intelligence startup Rebellions and participate in a question-and-answer session with Kakao Mobility. Rebellions said both engagements had been called off because of "unavoidable internal circumstances at Nvidia."South Korean media reported that Nvidia AI Day Seoul, a two-day conference expected to attract around 2,000 participants, would go ahead as scheduled. The event is set to focus on physical AI, agentic AI and infrastructure. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Impact on Nvidia and its sharesAccording to a Reuters report, trading in perpetual futures on the Hyperliquid exchange, along with after-hours share transactions on the Blue Ocean system, indicated that Nvidia shares were changing hands at around $178.60. This is a decline of more than 4% from the stock's closing price of $186.64 on the Nasdaq on Friday.Nvidia's chip technology has played a central role in several major shifts in the technology industry, spanning video gaming, autonomous vehicles, cloud computing and artificial intelligence.Huang's early decision to invest in AI proved significant. By the time ChatGPT was launched in late 2022, Nvidia's processors were already central to the computing infrastructure needed to meet the rapidly growing demand for AI applications.The company's market value has since climbed sharply, making it one of the world's most valuable businesses and an essential supplier to leading technology companies. Nvidia's valuation rose from $420 billion in late 2022 to $4.5 trillion as of November 6."The market's probably telling you now this does no favours ⁠to the stock whatsoever in a time when there's a lot of conjecture as to the build out of data centres," Chris Weston, head of research at brokerage Pepperstone in Melbourne told Reuters.However, Weston said he did not expect Huang, whom he described as the "godfather of AI", to be replaced."If we genuinely thought he was going to step down ... the stock would be down — it would be an absolute bloodbath, to be honest,” he said.The scrutiny of Huang's relationship with Alice Huang has emerged at a sensitive point for Nvidia. Investors are already questioning whether the AI boom that fuelled the company's extraordinary growth can be sustained. The board's investigation has added another layer of uncertainty by raising questions about the future of the executive most closely linked to Nvidia's success.The issue has also drawn attention from senior Republicans in the US House of Representatives, who have sought briefings from Huang following The New York Times report, pointing to concerns over national security.Nvidia has maintained that its board has "no reason to believe" that US national security or company secrets were compromised. However, an independent committee of directors will examine all the information available as part of its review.Analysts cautioned that an extended investigation or internal review could affect Nvidia's investment decisions and product launches, potentially creating wider repercussions for the semiconductor industry.Ryu Young-ho, a senior analyst at NH Investment & Securities, said competitors such as Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) could receive increased attention in the near term. This could also bring Samsung into greater focus because of its close business ties ⁠with AMD.However, Ryu said Nvidia's products would be difficult to replace, which could limit the overall impact of the developments. He added that shipments to China might face further delays, depending on how the situation unfolded.South Korea's deputy science minister said on Monday that the government did not expect any disruption to deliveries of Nvidia graphics processing units covered by existing contracts, despite the challenges currently confronting the company.Shares of Nvidia's major Asian chip suppliers recovered on Monday following last week's selloff in AI-related stocks. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) rose 6.5%, while Samsung Electronics gained 2.9% and SK Hynix advanced 4.7%.Several prominent personalities also commented on Huang's admission. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, who founded Pershing Square Capital Management, described the Nvidia chief executive as an "incredible human" in a post on X. However, he added that ‌if "indeed this is ⁠more than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem.""I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security," he added.Tesla CEO Elon Musk responded with "I agree" to a post by Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire. Maguire had said Huang "did something incredibly dumb" that was "bad for America", while also maintaining that "Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership".US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that he had not discussed the allegations with Huang. He nevertheless described the Nvidia CEO as a fine person. "I hope everything's fine. He's done such an incredible job," he added.Asked whether he believed he should have acted on the intelligence after being briefed about it, Trump said: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for ⁠it. You have to hear it."The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed on the intelligence findings approximately a year ago but decided against taking action based on the information.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Will have to return deposits’: Musk says Tesla will end Cybertruck production, rejects unprofitability claims
articles.summary: Tesla will have to refund deposits to a large number of customers who placed orders for its Cybertruck pickup, as demand has outstripped the company's
articles.body: Tesla will have to refund deposits to a large number of customers who placed orders for its Cybertruck pickup, as demand has outstripped the company's production capacity, CEO Elon Musk said. The electric vehicle maker plans to wind down production of the model at its Texas factory in about eight months to make room for its autonomous Cybercab.“We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people,” Musk said in a post on X on Monday, acknowledging that the Cybertruck's order rate was significantly higher than its production rate.Further rejecting unprofitability rumours, he added, "This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media, but rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production."The latest comments follow Musk's announcement last week that Tesla would add an extra production shift to clear outstanding Cybertruck orders before ending production. The manufacturing line is expected to be shut down around mid-2027, with resources redirected towards scaling up Cybercab output.Musk has rejected suggestions that the decision to discontinue the pickup was driven by profitability concerns. He argued that the complexity of manufacturing the Cybertruck made expanding its production less valuable than using the capacity to build more Cybercabs.“This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media, but rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production,” he said.Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in November 2019 and began customer deliveries in November 2023. Despite Musk's ambitious sales projections, the pickup has struggled to attract the expected demand. US sales fell 48 per cent to 20,237 units last year, according to Kelley Blue Book, far below Musk's earlier projection of annual sales reaching 250,000 vehicles.The Cybercab, unveiled in October 2024, is a two-seater autonomous electric vehicle designed without a steering wheel or pedals. articles.title: Nvidia's out-of-hour shares fall as firm probes CEO Jensen Huang
articles.summary: By Heekyong Yang, Kyu-seok Shim and Tom Westbrook SEOUL/SYDNEY, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Nvidia shares fell in out-of-hours trading on Monday after an internal inve...
articles.body:
By Heekyong Yang, Kyu-seok Shim and Tom Westbrook

SEOUL/SYDNEY, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock fell 4% during premarket trading on Monday after an internal investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort put his future at the AI chipmaker under scrutiny.

The internal probe followed a media report that Huang had a close ‌relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told Nvidia's employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the relationship.

The ‌investigation, announced on Sunday, has put a spotlight on Huang's future given Nvidia's status as the world's most valuable chipmaker and the CEO's role as the most prolific salesman of the AI boom.

The fallout extended to South Korea, where Madison Huang, Huang's ​daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled a planned visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference that was set to begin on Monday, according to companies she had been scheduled to meet.

Perpetual futures trading on the Hyperliquid exchange and after-hours shares trading on the Blue Ocean system showed Nvidia prices around $180.30 a share, down about 3.4% from Friday's Nasdaq closing price of $186.64.

"The market's probably telling you now this does no favours to the stock whatsoever in a time when there's a lot of conjecture as to the build out of data centres," said Chris Weston, head of research at brokerage Pepperstone in Melbourne.

But Weston said he did ‌not think Huang, whom he described as the "godfather of AI", would be ⁠replaced.

"If we genuinely thought he was going to step down ... the stock would be down — it would be an absolute bloodbath, to be honest," he said.

The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, who US authorities investigated ⁠and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Megaspeed did not respond immediately to a request for comment on Monday, a public holiday in Singapore.

Alice Huang did not respond to the New York Times last month when it first reported her relationship with Huang, and Reuters could not determine her location to seek comment on Monday.

Shares in Nvidia's key Asian chip suppliers TSMC, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix rebounded on Monday after last week's selloff ​of ​AI-related stocks. TSMC shares jumped 6.5%, while those in Samsung and SK Hynix climbed 2.9% and 4.7%, respectively.

articles.title: Jensen Huang just handed Wall Street its first $4.5 trillion CEO scandal
articles.summary: Wall Street has priced plenty of CEO scandals. It has never priced one at a company worth $4.5 trillion that makes up nearly 7% of the S&P 500.
articles.body:
Wall Street has priced plenty of CEO scandals. It has never priced one at a company worth $4.5 trillion that makes up nearly 7% of the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ).

Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang admitted in a Nov. 8 memo to employees to an affair with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence officials believe worked for China's Ministry of State Security. "I was unfaithful to my wife," he wrote. The board has opened an independent investigation.

Nvidia stock fell 5% before the bell on Monday following the news.

The scale is hard to overstate. At Friday's close, Nvidia was worth about four times the nine biggest companies ever hit by CEO personal-conduct scandals combined, by Yahoo Finance calculations. The largest, Intel ( INTC ), was worth $249 billion when Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 over a past consensual relationship with an employee. Nvidia is about 18 times that.

This is key-person risk — the danger that a company's value rests on one person — at its most extreme. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has run it ever since, with no named successor.

Adjust for a bigger stock market, and the gap narrows but doesn't close. No earlier scandal-hit company made up more than about 1% of the S&P 500, a mark only Intel in 2018 and HP ( HPQ ) in 2010 reached. Nvidia is about seven times that.

History puts a price on it. A 2018 study in the Journal of Financial Economics found stocks fell about 4% on average when the CEO was the one caught. At Nvidia's size, that's roughly $185 billion, more than McDonald's ( MCD ) was worth when it fired Steve Easterbrook in 2019.

So far, Wall Street has treated Nvidia like the safe chip stock.

Since Oct. 28, the last close before The New York Times' first spy report, Nvidia has fallen about 13%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) is down about 20% in a stretch that included a post-midterm rout. The gap holds from Nvidia's Oct. 6 record too.

Spy stories can hit hard. Super Micro Computer ( SMCI ) lost 41% in a day in 2018 on a report of Chinese spy chips in its servers, a report that was never confirmed.

The closer precedent may be Intel's Lip-Bu Tan. In August 2025, President Trump said Tan should resign over his China ties [1p link?]. Within a month, Washington had taken a stake in Intel and the stock was up about 20%.

This time, Trump is in the CEO's corner. "I think he's an honorable guy," he told reporters Sunday.

Options traders were braced even before the admission. Friday's prices implied a move of more than 3% either way for Monday alone, more than double Nvidia's typical day lately.

articles.title: Luxury brands try to entice younger consumers with new experiences
articles.summary: Attending a legacy luxury brand’s workshop is “almost like being at a museum-level exhibit” because of the history on display, said a marketing professor.
articles.body: On a recent afternoon in New York City, a small group watched as craftspeople in lab coats cleaned and carved small silver pieces under microscopes. One by one, they peered through a magnifying glass at the glittering golden plume of a diamond bird. There was a loud gasp when a 3D-printed necklace was revealed. At Tiffany & Co.’s Jewelry Innovation & Design workshop, the guests — some visiting from Belgium, India and Brazil — were given a front row seat to the jewelry maker’s craftspeople at work. Many staffers had worked at Tiffany’s for decades, showing off their “traditional tools,” including a wall of hammers — some of which were over a century old. Fashion Institute of Technology student Isabelle Eilenkrig-Turnier and her mother, Inga Eilenkrig, had been interested in these types of luxury exhibits since visiting a Christian Dior factory in Florence, where Isabelle was a student. “One thing is to see the beauty. But it’s also the ability to see how much actually goes into (making) it,” Inga said. Such glimpses into product innovation could revive customer trust for legacy brands after severe price hikes pushed young and aspirational buyers towards upstarts or buying second-hand. Luxury prices have soared in recent years, rising an average 61% between 2019 and 2025 according to McKinsey & Co.’s State of Fashion report. Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton (LVMH), the owner of Tiffany’s, isn’t the only company pulling out all the stops to convince shoppers that their products are worth the price. Gucci has hosted museum-like exhibits covering its 105-year history. Chanel founded an art space in 2021, Galerie du 19m, displaying the craftsmanship behind luxury goods. LVMH also introduced customers to the artisans and processes behind its other brands — including Loewe in Spain and Hennessy in France. The luxury industry “is not exactly thriving right now,” said Antoine Arnault, LVMH’s director of image and environment, “but that’s not the reason we’re doing (Les Journées Particulières).” “Les Journées Particulières,” the brainchild of Arnault, son of LVMH chief executive Bernard Arnault, was created in 2011 to spotlight the company’s artisans. “It’s almost like being at a museum-level exhibit,” said Thomaï Serdari, a marketing professor at New York University, of LVMH’s workshops. Events like the one at Tiffany’s can reinforce the idea of a brand’s history and purpose, she said. LVMH could use a boost. The company’s revenue fell about 5% to $80.8 billion in 2025, according to the company, marking two years of revenue declines. Experiences shape a competitive market Les Journées Particulières is an effort to not only lift the curtain on the exclusive world of luxury design, but also draw new customers in. The program shows shoppers how and where products are made, conceived after a period where luxury brands, including LVMH, faced accusations of producing goods in China to cut costs, says Bernstein analyst Luca Solca. But brands like Chanel and LVMH are also looking to expand their customer base to less wealthy clientele, Solca said. Middle-class shoppers represent more than half of the market, and transparency about how products are made can attract customers, he said. “The sooner brands find the appropriate mix to reconnect with the aspirational middle-class consumers, the better,” he said. Post-pandemic price hikes damaged customer trust, said Gemma D’Auria, senior partner and global leader of luxury at McKinsey & Co, as customers questioned whether product quality matched higher costs. Companies raised prices to both capitalize on pandemic-era splurging and offset higher fuel and manufacturing expenses in 2022. But that priced out aspirational buyers — those who buy lower-priced products or younger professionals. Those customers account for about half of sales for the luxury market, and they are now looking to newer brands. McKinsey found that most American luxury clients (66%) say challenger brands — smaller, independent fashion houses with less established history — feel more exclusive than legacy brands. “Luxury brands need to re-arm this trust through transparency, through product quality,” D’Auria said. “This is why these experiences become a competitive differentiator.” Events are a “value creation,” says Silvia Bellezza, a marketing professor at Columbia University. Her research has found that learning about the manufacturing process can make people more willing to commit to a purchase. “Every opportunity that you have to impress your customers when you have them physically in store, you have to use it,” said Bellezza. At the Tiffany & Co. workshop, Eleonore Trevisan, a student at Columbia University originally from Luxembourg, attended the event with her boyfriend, a longtime shareholder of Tiffany’s. She told CNN after the experience that it was important to keep “craftsmanship in culture.” She one day hopes to buy a Tiffany product. “It’s a brand that makes me dream,” Trevisan said.

articles.title: Sudan teachers go on strike over meagre salaries and dilapidated schools
articles.summary: Teachers across the country say their pay no longer covers basic living costs.
articles.body:
Khartoum, Sudan – For 26 years, Amal Suleiman Ahmed al-Haj has worked as a secondary school teacher in Sudan.

But her monthly salary of 132,000 Sudanese pounds ($13.20) only covers her family’s basic needs for a few days. Just buying a cooking gas cylinder will set her back about 170,000 pounds ($17).

With teachers in Khartoum State no longer paid enough to survive, they have gone on strike for a third week.

“My salary does not cover even a quarter of our needs. It may not last a family more than three or four days,” Amal told Al Jazeera. “Teachers are extremely exhausted and have to find other jobs in the evenings to supplement their income. In reality, we have become secondary workers in the education sector.”

Beyond their salary issues, teachers are also unhappy with the lack of opportunities for promotion and accumulated unpaid entitlements.

They are also worried about deteriorating conditions in schools, caused by war and a lack of investment. Some classrooms at Amal’s school are no longer suitable for teaching.

“There is a classroom where I teach and its roof has collapsed, leaving us directly exposed to the sun. This is the environment in which we teach, and it affects both us and the students,” Amal told Al Jazeera.

“Those of us who stayed in Sudan [during the war] lost out. We did not lose our jobs, but we were not working and were not receiving salaries. As a result, our outstanding payments accumulated with the government.”

Amal said that teachers have resorted to strike action after exhausting all official channels to demand their rights.

“We submitted memorandums to the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance and the presidential palace, but nothing came of it. We also spoke through the media, and there was no solution left except going on strike,” she said.

“How can a teacher educate students when they cannot afford to get to school, pay for transport or provide for their children?” she said.

Many teachers Amal knows are considering leaving the profession. Some have already quit their jobs, taken unpaid leave, or sought alternative sources of income.

Amal admits that the suspension of classes during the strike is negatively affecting her students. But with Sudan’s education system in crisis, she says teachers need at least the basic conditions necessary to do their jobs.

“Teachers are human beings. They have needs, families and responsibilities. How can they fulfil their educational mission under these pressures? Some teachers walk long distances to reach their schools, while others faint because of malnutrition and exhaustion,” she said.

“We are not asking for luxuries. We just want to be able to live, get to our schools and continue our educational mission.”

The Sudanese Teachers’ Committee has organised staggered, intermittent strikes to pressure the government into addressing teachers’ demands.

Sami al-Baqir, the committee’s spokesperson, said participation was initially widespread, but later declined after alleged attempts by the government to undermine the industrial action. The measures included relaxing administrative controls over staff attendance to make schools appear operational despite the strikes and providing model schools with mechanisms to generate additional funding. Some teachers also received partial outstanding payments from the government when new strikes were announced.

After a meeting between Sudanese ministers and unions last month, Prime Minister Kamil Idris ordered the payment of money owed to teachers across all Sudanese states. However, the government did not give a detailed payment schedule or address teachers’ other demands concerning salaries and allowances, leading to the continued impasse.

The Sudanese teachers’ union says it is braced for a long battle to resolve its members’ grievances.

“We called … [for] a long-haul strike to absorb the tactics the government is using. It tries to circumvent the problems rather than solve them,” al-Baqir told Al Jazeera.

Their demands include an increase in the minimum wage from 12,000 Sudanese pounds ($1.20) to 500,000 pounds ($50), based on poverty-line benchmarks and a cost-of-living study for a family of five conducted by the Sudanese Teachers’ Committee.

The body also wants three cabinet decisions made more than seven months ago to be implemented, including an increase in the meal allowance to 90,000 pounds ($9), the introduction of a housing allowance, and a 130,000-pound ($13) allowance to address salary disparities among public sector employees.

“These decisions were issued by the cabinet, but they have not been implemented so far. This indicates that the government is not serious about addressing teachers’ problems,” al-Baqir said.

The ongoing war between the Sudanese army and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which broke out in April 2023, has contributed to the problems faced by teachers and school administrators, al-Baqir explained.

“For schools to reopen, teachers to return and the education system to stabilise, the problems facing schools and teachers must be addressed,” he added.

The conflict has disrupted schooling, destroyed educational facilities and turned some into shelters for the displaced or military sites, depriving millions of children of access to education.

The UN has documented 67 attacks on schools in Sudan since 2024, alongside more than 150 reports of armed groups commandeering educational facilities.

Lily Neyestani-Hailu, head of education in emergencies at UNESCO, said the conflict had forced hundreds of thousands of children out of school and put millions more at risk of missing out on education.

She said about 30 percent of Sudan’s schools were damaged or closed due to the war and more than 1,400 schools had been attacked.

Other estimates say that nearly half of the country’s schools are not functioning because of war damage or because they are being used as shelters or military facilities.

According to Sudan Education Cluster data published in January, 97 percent of schools in North Darfur have stopped classes. Only 13 percent of schools are operational in South Darfur and just 27 percent in West Darfur – two of the areas that have been worst-hit by the war.

At least 8 million children are now out of school, according to the UN, with poverty-stricken parents sending their children to work to help cover rising living costs.

School closures, a lack of investment in education and underpaid teachers are putting huge pressure on Sudan’s public education system.

“We are genuinely afraid that public education will be phased out,” al-Baqir said. “The government’s disregard for teachers’ rights, its failure to spend on education and the current administrative disorder in schools all send a message to parents that anyone who can afford private education will take their children there.”

articles.title: Woman visited bank to access locker, but found it surrendered without knowledge despite rent payments; commission orders bank to pay Rs 47 lakh for missing jewellery, 6% interest and Rs 3.5 lakh costs
articles.summary: Can your bank locker be surrendered without you being aware?
articles.body: Can your bank locker be surrendered without you being aware? And is the bank liable then for items you claim were in the locker that was surrendered without your knowledge?In one such case, a woman who tried to access a joint locker was told by the concerned bank that the locker had already been surrendered.Now, the Delhi State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has directed the bank to pay her compensation for the jewellery she said was missing, along with interest, and mental agony and harassment, and litigation costs.The commission found that the bank had failed to produce records establishing that the locker had been properly surrendered or that its contents had been returned. It rejected the bank’s claim that the locker had been surrendered several years ago, noting that locker rent continued to be debited even years later.What the case is aboutA woman held a joint locker with her father-in-law at a bank in Delhi. According to the complaint, the locker arrangement dated back to 1998. Her father-in-law, who operated the locker in 2005, died on August 29, 2010.On September 1, 2018, the woman approached the bank to access the locker. She alleged that the bank informed her it had been surrendered on January 22, 2015. She maintained that she had never requested its surrender and had received no notice that the locker had been closed or allotted to another customer.The woman claimed that jewellery worth approximately Rs 47 lakh was missing from the locker. Alleging deficiency in banking services, she filed a consumer complaint in 2019, seeking the value of the jewellery with interest, compensation for mental agony and litigation expenses.The bank disputed her allegations. In its written statement, it claimed that the locker had been surrendered on May 21, 2005. It described the continued deduction of locker rent as a bona fide mistake and argued that it accepted only empty lockers when customers surrendered them. It also challenged the commission’s jurisdiction and maintained that the complaint was time-barred.Why the commission ruled in favour of locker holderThe commission first rejected the bank’s jurisdictional objections. It noted that the woman had claimed Rs 48 lakh in total compensation, bringing the complaint within its pecuniary jurisdiction under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. The bank’s Naraina Vihar branch was in Delhi, giving the commission territorial jurisdiction as well.On the main dispute, the commission examined the bank records showing that locker rent continued to be debited from the woman’s account, including on September 25, 2018. It found that the bank had not produced a receipt establishing the locker’s surrender.The commission observed: “Even if the mistake on the part of the Opposite Party Bank was Bonafide, the Opposite Party has also failed to place on record any receipt of surrender of the locker in question”.It also found no evidence that the woman had communicated a request to surrender the locker. Nor had the bank produced a receipt showing that the jewellery or other contents had been handed over when it claimed the locker was closed.As the order states: “Further, there is no receipt of the items in the locker of the Complainant and her deceased father-in-law provided by the Opposite Party at the time of the alleged surrender of the said locker”.On that basis, the commission rejected the bank’s contention that the locker had been surrendered on May 21, 2005. It concluded that the bank had failed to establish that the woman had surrendered the locker or received its contents back. The commission held that “the belongings of the Complainant were misappropriated by the Opposite Party”.The commission directed the bank to pay Rs 47 lakh, with simple interest at 6% per annum calculated from September 1, 2018, to October 27, 2026, provided payment was made by December 27, 2026. If the bank failed to pay by that deadline, the amount would carry interest at 9% per annum from September 1, 2018, until realisation.The bank was also directed to pay Rs 3 lakh for mental agony and harassment and Rs 50,000 towards litigation costs.According to Amitraj Kaushal, Advocate at Supreme Court of India, the RBI's directions on safe deposit lockers lay down a prescribed procedure that banks must follow, including giving prior notice before terminating a locker agreement or opening a locker.Surrendering a locker is generally a formal process involving both the bank and the customer. It ordinarily requires a written request from the customer, along with the return of the locker key and an acknowledgement of the handover.“Silence from the customer is not consent. A surrender done without informing you can be challenged as deficiency in service,” he told ET.“Rent was still being debited from her account which shows the locker was live in the bank records. The Commission treated this as deficiency in service and held that the jewellery had been misappropriated by the bank,” explained Amritraj Kaushal.What documents should you preserve for your bank locker?Keeping records of financial transactions and important agreements is essential, and a bank locker is no exception. Kaushal advised customers to retain their locker agreement and all receipts for rent payments.“Bank statements showing the rent debits were relied on by the Commission in this case so save them too.”Customers should also make it a point to visit their lockers at least once a year and maintain a record of each visit. Before placing valuables inside, they should take photographs bearing the date and keep purchase invoices or valuation documents at home rather than storing them in the locker.If a joint locker holder dies, the bank should be informed in writing and the necessary formalities completed promptly. Similarly, anyone surrendering a locker should obtain a surrender receipt signed by the bank, ensure that it mentions the date and subsequently verify that locker rent is no longer being deducted.You use AI every day. articles.title: Gas is about to drop below $4 for the first time since July
articles.summary: Seasonal factors will reduce demand for gasoline, driving prices lower. But don’t expect prices to reach pre-Iran war levels anytime soon.
articles.body: Here’s a sight for voters’ sore eyes: nearly $4 gas. The average price of gas is poised to fall below that threshold for the first time since July, driven lower by seasonal factors that are reducing demand. The national average price for a gallon of gasoline early Monday was about $4.01, according to data from AAA. That’s down roughly 14 cents since Election Day, when it stood at $4.15 a gallon, and down 36 cents, or a little more than 8%, from a month ago when the price stood around $4.37. There are 26 states with an average price already below $4, with North Carolina having the lowest average at $3.26. Few issues were more important to voters this year than the cost of living, and high gas prices were a critical and visible component of those concerns. CNN polling conducted from October through Election Day showed 87% of voters were at least somewhat concerned with high gas prices, with six in 10 saying they were “very concerned.” But experts warn that Americans should not expect gasoline to approach the pre-Iran war level of $2.98 a gallon anytime soon, let alone the sub $2-a-gallon gas that President Donald Trump promised on the 2024 campaign trail. Why prices are falling Two seasonal factors have helped drive down demand for gasoline: the end of both the summer driving season and Daylight Saving Time. Americans drive less when it’s dark, so earlier darkness means fewer miles on the road. And with increasingly earlier sunsets through December 21, demand will continue to cool. Yet those factors don’t have as much impact on diesel fuel and jet fuel, which typically remain in higher demand during the colder seasons. Diesel is used for trucking and farming equipment and is also the same basic product as home heating oil. Meanwhile, US-based airlines are reporting strong appetite for travel through the end of the year. Diesel and jet fuel prices have stayed much closer to their peaks. Diesel prices hit a record of $6.52 on September 22 and are down only about 5% since then. Spot jet fuel prices are down about 2% in the same period. The average price of gasoline, meanwhile, is down about 10% in the same seven-week period. That higher demand for diesel and jet fuel has kept oil refineries running at maximum speed, which, in turn, has benefitted gasoline. A single barrel of crude oil is turned into myriad products—including diesel, jet fuel and gas—meaning the ramp up in production has also boosted gasoline supplies. “(Refineries are) operating at higher utilization than this time last year to make all the jet fuel and diesel fuel they can, and that makes gasoline really a byproduct, contributing to higher inventories,” said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. Trouble ahead in 2027? Gas may stay below $4 a gallon throughout the next few months—even without a lasting truce in the war in Iran, Lipow said. But even if a truce materializes, gas prices could stay well above $3 a gallon for the foreseeable future. That’s due to the more lasting damage done to the world’s refinery capacity from fighting in Russia and the Middle East. “There’s 7 million barrels a day of refined products capacity that’s been knocked out by drones or missiles, and that’s not likely to return soon,” said Tom Kloza, an independent oil analyst and an advisor to Gulf Oil. As a result, gas prices could rise above $4 a gallon next spring—a move that is likely to agitate Americans again. A survey published by AAA in 2022 found that $4 gas is considered a tipping point for drivers, with 59% of respondents saying they would make changes to their lifestyle or driving habits if prices rose to that level. “People might be talking at cocktail parties at Christmas about, ‘Oh, I only paid $3.50 a gallon today,’” Kloza said. “But watch out next spring — we’re going to go sharply higher.” Looking further down the line, prices could face more upward pressure as oil companies catch up on deferred maintenance of their refineries. ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told investors earlier this year that the company had deferred maintenance, which helped maintain output and profitability. But those deferrals can’t last forever—meaning that prices could rise as refineries go offline. Kloza says that major oil companies privately talk of how 2027 will be “the mother of all refinery maintenance years.” Another factor that could keep gas prices high, Kloza added: Gas station owners recalibrating their prices. The final price that Americans pay at the pump is set by thousands of gas station owners, who base their pricing on the wholesale prices they pay, while factoring in the prices of nearby competitors. During a spike in wholesale gasoline prices, some station owners will actually absorb a temporary loss of profits, even if their customers see a rapid increase in prices, so they don’t lose business to rival stations that might have bought gas before the latest rise in wholesale prices. But when wholesale prices fall, as they have recently, station owners are often slow to lower prices as they try to recoup losses from periods when prices were climbing. It reinforces the industry maxim that “prices go up like a rocket but come down like a feather.” Kloza said the recent drop in prices has been fairly rapid by historical standards. “It’s still a feather, but it’s more of a wet feather,” he said.

articles.title: Eggs and chicken may cost 25-30% more by December; eggs could hit Rs 8 per piece and without skin dressed chicken Rs 275 per kg as maize and broken rice prices surge
articles.summary: Your meal costs may go up in December as egg and chicken prices could rise by 25-30%.
articles.body: Your meal costs may go up in December as egg and chicken prices could rise by 25-30%. This is because the cost of poultry feed ingredients, including maize and broken rice, has climbed 30-45% over the past month compared with the same period a year ago.Maize and broken rice prices have doubled in the past year. With farmers and traders holding back maize stocks, the industry that uses the grain as a key raw material expects the upward price trend to continue through December.Eggs, chicken to get costlier as feed prices go upWholesale egg prices, currently hovering at Rs 6-7 per egg, are projected to climb to Rs 7-8 by December. The wholesale rate of dressed chicken without skin is also expected to rise from the current Rs 225-250 per kg to Rs 260-275 per kg over the same period, according to senior industry executives.December and January are among the busiest months for poultry consumption, with demand typically rising during the Christmas and New Year festivities.Maize, which cost around Rs 18 per kg last year, is now selling at Rs 34 per kg. Prices were in the range of Rs 26-27 per kg just a month ago, according to an ET report.Industry participants fear that the rate could reach Rs 40 per kg by December, as intermediaries in the supply chain stockpile the commodity in anticipation of further price increases.Broken rice has also become significantly more expensive. Its price, which stood at Rs 14-15 per kg around November 2025, has risen to Rs 31-32 per kg. A month ago, it was available at approximately Rs 22-23 per kg, according to trade data.Industry estimates suggest that a deficient monsoon in Maharashtra and Karnataka, two important kharif maize-producing states, could lead to a 15-16% decline in India's kharif maize output."Earlier, whenever prices of maize and rice increased, we used to shift to other cereals like jowar, bajra, ragi etc. However, even these cereals are expensive to use in poultry feed now," KG Anand, general manager of Venkateshwara Hatcheries told the financial daily."Although the increase in production costs has been high, we cannot pass the entire increase in costs to the consumers," said Anand."This year, we are expecting the production to fall by more than 20% during December and January as farmers are likely to sell younger birds in order to reduce the cost of feeding them," said Anand.Maize prices have continued to rise amid a growing diversion of the grain towards ethanol production. articles.title: Google's chip business is on a faster track than Nvidia's own AI boom
articles.summary: As Nvidia investigates its CEO, Google is rolling out more chips built to win Nvidia's customers on price.
articles.body:
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is investigating its own CEO. Google is busy building the chips that could take its customers.

Nvidia quickly sunk 8% after the opening bell Monday, trading at its lowest level since March, as its board looks into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy . Alphabet ( GOOGL ) is up about 3%. It's the latest chapter in Wall Street's first $4.5 trillion CEO scandal .

Google introduced two new tensor processing units, or TPUs — its homegrown AI chips — on Monday. The TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max join the 8t and 8i it unveiled in April, the first time Google has introduced four TPU systems in a single year. Both new chips ship next year.

Think of it as a chip menu. The 8tx keeps data encrypted for governments, banks, and other regulated businesses, paired with processors from AMD ( AMD ). The 8i Max squeezes two chips into one package for requests with long context windows — the amount of information an AI model can juggle at once.

The forecasts are the eye-popper. Bloomberg Intelligence sees TPU sales rising from about $12 billion this year to more than $135 billion by 2028, not counting chips rented through Google Cloud. That's more than 11-fold in two years.

Nvidia's data center business grew nearly eightfold in the first two years of the AI boom, from $15 billion in fiscal 2023 to $115 billion in fiscal 2025.

The chips are already flying off the line. Epoch AI estimates TPU shipments doubled in computing power in a single quarter this year, to roughly 800,000 chips.

Anthropic is the headliner. Its IPO filing shows about $161 billion of lease payments tied to TPUs, which Raymond James says makes it the biggest custom-chip customer of Google's design partner, Broadcom ( AVGO ). Meta ( META ), OpenAI and Oracle ( ORCL ) are buyers too.

Google used to roll out about one data center TPU a year. Now it has one for every job.

Its next-generation Rubin chip is rated at 35 petaflops — a measure of raw computing speed — compared with about 10 for Google's 8i and about 20 for the 8i Max, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.

Google is selling on price. SemiAnalysis found that Google's current Ironwood TPU delivers up to nearly three times as much AI output per dollar as Nvidia's Blackwell chips when running AI agents, though Nvidia's top system still wins when speed is everything.

Forecasts aren't sales, and Nvidia still sells far more AI chips than anyone else.

Nvidia's next big moment comes Nov. 17, when it reports third quarter results, a day before a requested closed-door House briefing on CEO Jensen Huang . Investors will want to hear whether customers are hedging their bets. As Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon wrote to clients, "Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS NVIDIA."

articles.title: TED JENKIN: Europe is burning because people can't pay their bills. America should pay attention
articles.summary: There's no Facebook or TikTok needed when families can't afford groceries, housing and healthcare, and a paycheck is already spoken for.
articles.body: In 1789, angry French citizens didn't have Facebook, Instagram or TikTok to complain about the cost of living. They had pitchforks. And torches. When bread prices became unbearable, thousands of women marched on the Palace of Versailles, demanding answers from King Louis XVI. They weren't marching because the stock market was down. They were marching because they couldn't afford to feed their families. GORDON SONDLAND: FRANCE IS BURNING, EUROPE'S BROKE, AND THE REVOLUTION IT REALLY NEEDS ISN'T VIOLENT More than 230 years later, France is once again witnessing angry crowds in the streets. Italy has seen tens of thousands of workers and students protesting over wages, housing and living costs. The circumstances are different. The frustration sounds remarkably familiar. People are working, collecting paychecks and wondering why they still can't afford their lives. MELONI CONDEMNS ‘GANGS OF THUGS’ AFTER PROTESTS TURNED VIOLENT ACROSS ITALY And America had better pay attention. The economy looks great until you open your wallet Politicians love talking about economic growth, unemployment rates and inflation statistics. But here's a little secret. Most Americans don't wake up in the morning wondering what happened to GDP. They wonder whether they can afford groceries, pay the electric bill and make their mortgage payment. And there's an enormous difference between what economists call a healthy economy and what families experience at their kitchen tables. MEHEK COOKE: REPUBLICANS FAILED THE AFFORDABILITY TEST. THIS IS HOW TO WIN VOTERS BACK Inflation might fall from 8% to 3%. Wonderful. That doesn't mean your $200 grocery bill goes back to $150. It means prices are generally rising more slowly. Your paycheck may have increased, but so have your insurance premiums, property taxes, utilities and rent. The result? You can earn more money and still feel poorer. EJ ANTONI: OVERSEAS WARS PUT AFFORDABILITY ON HOLD, BUT THAT’S ONLY TEMPORARY Europe's warning sign France has experienced protests over living costs, public services and government finances. Italy has seen workers and students march over wages, housing affordability and their economic futures. Not every protest is about household bills, and most demonstrators aren't rioters. THOUSANDS FLOOD BRUSSELS STREETS AS ANTI-AUSTERITY PROTESTS ERUPT INTO CLASHES WITH POLICE But the financial frustration deserves attention. Politicians love talking about economic growth, unemployment rates and inflation statistics. But here's a little secret. Most Americans don't wake up in the morning wondering what happened to GDP. When people believe working hard no longer guarantees a reasonable standard of living, something changes. They stop believing the economic promises. They stop trusting the statistics. DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE And eventually, some take their anger into the streets. Financial stress doesn't disappear just because a government says inflation is under control. AMERICANS SAY THEY'RE BROKE. SO WHY CAN'T THEY STOP SPENDING SO MUCH? America has its own powder keg Think about the financial pressure facing an American family today. A young couple wants to buy their first home but can't save a down payment fast enough to keep up with housing costs. Parents earn decent salaries but struggle with childcare, groceries, the cost of college and health insurance. Retirees on fixed incomes watch property taxes and insurance premiums eat into their savings and Social Security checks. Meanwhile, credit cards become the emergency fund. Buy now, pay later becomes the family budgeting strategy. And everyone wonders why they feel financially exhausted. Here's the problem. You can't build long-term financial stability when every paycheck is already spoken for. Government debt makes the problem harder France's fiscal troubles illustrate another uncomfortable reality. When governments accumulate enormous debt, interest payments compete with spending on services and other priorities. America has now crossed $40 trillion in federal debt. That doesn't mean the United States is about to experience the French Revolution. But it does mean Washington has less room to respond to future economic shocks without difficult decisions about borrowing, taxes and spending. And households ultimately live with the consequences of those decisions. The real measure of affordability Here's what I'd like every politician in America to answer. After a family pays for housing, food, transportation, healthcare and utilities, how much money is actually left? Not how much their wages increased on paper. Not whether inflation came down two percentage points. How much is left? Because that remaining money determines whether families can save, invest, take a vacation or handle an emergency without going into debt. If we want to improve affordability, we need more housing, stronger opportunities for wage growth, competitive markets and fiscal discipline. And families need to understand where their money is going before debt becomes their only option. Meanwhile, credit cards become the emergency fund. Buy now, pay later becomes the family budgeting strategy. And everyone wonders why they feel financially exhausted. In 1789, the French marched on Versailles demanding bread. Today, families across Europe are demanding economic security. Americans are asking many of the same questions. articles.title: Nvidia is in peril. Can it survive without Jensen Huang?
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he wants to die at his desk. He frequently talks about how integral he is to the foundation of the world’s second-biggest company and the world’s most important AI chipmaker.
articles.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he wants to die at his desk. He frequently talks about how integral he is to the foundation of the world’s second-biggest company and the world’s most important AI chipmaker. Soon, Nvidia may need to learn how to live without its CEO of 33 years. Huang’s extramarital affair with a customer whom Nvidia is investigating for potential espionage threatens to oust him from the CEO role he has held since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. The extraordinary revelation Sunday raises the specter of an AI earthquake: An Nvidia without Huang, who helped form the bedrock of AI computing power that fuels the revolutionary technology transforming the global economy. The investigation has just begun, and Huang’s future remains unclear. So too does the future of Nvidia. Nvidia without Jensen? Huang admitted to an extramarital affair Sunday as his company announced it would investigate reports he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The separate statements came amid growing concern over his relationship with an executive from Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed, Alice Huang. Several US outlets have reported that American officials suspect Alice Huang, no relation, fed intelligence to China and helped smuggle advanced artificial intelligence chips into the country. The New York Times first reported on their relationship, showing Alice Huang photographed with Jensen Huang, the silver-haired CEO wearing his signature leather jacket, who has become one of the faces of AI. The board inquiry is especially striking given Huang’s close relationship with President Donald Trump and central role in advising on AI policy, where he has pushed for fewer restrictions on trade of advanced American technology to China. He traveled with Trump to China earlier this year and the Middle East last year. He was seated next to the president at a White House lunch in September, during which AI and political leaders formed an accord for how the companies should “self-police” for AI risks. Investors are concerned about Nvidia’s future — and Huang’s potential departure: The company’s stock fell 6% Monday. “Losing Huang would introduce a lot of uncertainty, particularly given his influence over Nvidia’s strategy, culture, and relationships with major technology companies,” said Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. “The stock would be in even tougher shape than it is now if that were to happen. He is an exceptionally important figure to tech and the AI buildout.” Jensen = Nvidia “Our company was built so that I know how to run it. So, for as long as I’m running it, that’s all that matters.” Three and a half years have passed since Huang gave that quote to Bloomberg, and he has become only more interwoven with the fabric of Nvidia as demand for the company’s AI chips has exploded in value. Today, Nvidia is worth $4.5 trillion — roughly two years after it surpassed a $1 trillion valuation. Huang’s longevity partly stems from a myth he’s created for himself that extends back to Nvidia’s creation story: He and the company’s co-founders sat at a Denny’s in 1993 and sketched out the business plan for the chip company. According to Huang’s telling, the co-founders told Huang he’d be responsible for running the business to do the stuff they didn’t understand. Huang also loves to talk about how he repeatedly saved the company from near death — so much that the company’s motto, emblazoned on slide decks and topping presentations, was: “Our company is thirty days from going out of business.” Nvidia executives who have spoken about Huang talk about a tough, chronically frustrated boss who publicly berates his staff in front of others. Yet Huang also has a disarming sense of humor and some endearing quirks (like not wearing a watch, because the most important time is now.) He’s gotten Nvidia’s staff to be fiercely loyal to him. Huang prides himself on outlasting his peers. He is fond of poking fun at other CEOs, telling them that when their children are running their companies, Huang will still be running Nvidia. Huang has said he never believed in succession planning, telling podcaster Lex Fridman earlier this year that he hoped to die at his desk. That Steve Jobs-like reality distortion field extends to the aura he constructed that convinced many inside and outside Nvidia that Huang can tell the future — most notably being spot on (and way early) about the company’s graphics processors serving as the bedrock for AI. That was in 2013, a decade before ChatGPT. In 2016, Nvidia donated a supercomputer powered by its GPUs to OpenAI. Whether Nvidia’s success is attributable to Huang’s luck, unique intelligence or both, it’s clear that Nvidia’s success is because of Huang. The investigation “brings the stewardship of one of America’s most important companies, and the architect of the US AI trajectory, under debate,” Stacy Rasgon, senior analyst covering semiconductors at Bernstein Research, said in a note on Monday. If Huang isn’t CEO, what becomes of Nvidia? Nvidia’s board has said it currently has no reason to believe that US national security or Nvidia’s secrets were compromised. And Huang has committed to continuing to lead the company. Still, the board “absolutely has an obligation to investigate this quite thoroughly” and remove Huang if he were indeed found to have shared private information about the company, said Kathy Harrigan, professor of business leadership at Columbia Business School. And while Huang and Nvidia may not have publicly discussed succession planning, “a competent board would have had at least two individuals in training, or a pretty good idea about what kind of person they would want to recruit from the outside if it were necessary,” Harrigan said. “Boards are there to protect shareholders, and they have to see to it that, just in case he gets hit by a truck tomorrow, the company will continue on,” she added. The board is in a tricky position — it’s obligated to fully investigate the situation, but if the inquiry uncovers evidence of harm to the company, it could increase Nvidia’s exposure to shareholder lawsuits, said Ann Lipton, professor at Colorado Law School at the University of Colorado, Boulder. Nvidia previously downplayed Huang’s connection to Megaspeed, statements that could come back to bite the company in a potential fraud lawsuit, in which shareholders could seek compensation for the stock’s decline if they can prove that Huang or the company made intentional misstatements about the incident and the risks it posed to Nvidia. Such claims could be filed within days, Lipton said. Shareholders could also seek to sue for breach of fiduciary duty, although those claims could be harder to substantiate. Currently, the company is at “pretty severe risk” of shareholder litigation, she said. No business — even one with a singular leader like Nvidia’s — is exclusively dependent on one person, noted Mahoney. Long term, Nvidia could lose a competitive advantage, but demand for the company’s chips won’t evaporate immediately if Huang is ousted. And despite Huang’s leadership style, Nvidia’s bench is deep. Just like Apple without Steve Jobs, the company can continue without Huang. “The same is true with Nvidia as it was with Apple: Their competitive advantages extend well beyond one individual,” Mahoney said. “The bigger question is whether a successor could maintain Huang’s strategic vision and ability to anticipate where the industry is heading – and how that new leader could be tested along the way if things become difficult.” Other analysts echoed that while the investigation creates uncertainty for Nvidia and the surrounding industry in the short-term, it would be unlikely to entirely upend the company’s business. Major firms buying Nvidia’s chips and software for AI training and data centers are unlikely to slash “their capital spending amid uncertainty around the Nvidia CEO position,” Morningstar Senior Equity Analyst Brian Colello said in an email. However, he added that Huang has played a central role in mobilizing funding for the AI buildout — helping other companies afford to buy his chips — and said the “costs of capital may rise for future investments if perhaps the most prominent CEO in the AI landscape is no longer orchestrating such deals.”

articles.title: Nvidia stock falls after company opens probe into CEO’s relationship with Chinese spy
articles.summary: Nvidia’s stock slid after the company announced that it had opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
articles.body: Nvidia’s stock slid about 5% on Monday after the company announced that it had opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman that U.S. intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. The probe has the potential to unsettle the entire AI boom, fueled by trillions of dollars of spending and investments, in part to purchase Nvidia’s cutting-edge AI chips. Nvidia’s drop wiped out more than $240 billion in value. The CEO, who also founded the company more than three decades ago, admitted in a note to employees he had been unfaithful to his wife. “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” Huang’s email also said. In recent days, the Financial Times and The New York Times reported that Huang had a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang. A person with knowledge of the matter told NBC News that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. The two Huangs are unrelated. China has dismissed the espionage allegations as a “smears.” The company where Alice Huang allegedly works, Megaspeed, did not return requests for comment. Nvidia said in a Sunday statement that independent directors and counsel will oversee the probe. “The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. An Nvidia spokesperson told NBC News that Huang was “committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption.” Despite Nvidia’s importance to the AI trade, the news affected almost no other stocks. The Nasdaq 100, which tracks the top tech stocks at the Nasdaq exchange, soared 3.3%. The broader S&P 500 rose 2.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose more than 1,000 points. Stocks were also propelled higher by a sharp 5% drop in oil prices on Monday, on news that U.S. and Iran talks were continuing. Trump also told CNN on Sunday that it would be “highly unlikely” that he would restart major combat operations against Iran. Nvidia’s peers, such as AMD, Qualcomm, Taiwan Semi and Intel, all rose along with the broader market. Nvidia was the biggest loser on the Dow and S&P 500. Before the Huang revelations, the tech industry was on edge, with every headline about AI-linked companies sending stocks either soaring or tumbling. Just last week, tech stocks surged after it became clear on Election Night that the Democrats would win majorities in Congress. But stocks plunged the next day. On Thursday, stocks suffered their worst one-day drop since Trump rocked the global economy with his initial wave of tariffs in April 2025. Given that there are few more important companies to the tech sector overall, investors and even market watchers not invested in Nvidia shares will be closely following the investigation. There are still many unanswered questions. On Sunday, Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” But, it did not provide a timeline related to how fast the probe would be conducted or any other details about Huang’s contact with Alice Huang. Jensen Huang’s influence Jensen Huang has become one of the main forces driving the global AI push while steering Nvidia to a market value of more than $4 trillion. Huang has led Nvidia since he founded it in 1993, so it would be a seismic change if he were to leave the role. Huang is the largest individual holder of shares, outside of investment funds, and he is not protected from removal if the board decides to do so. His stake in shares of Nvidia are worth about 3.5% of its shares outstanding, but unlike other major tech firms like Meta, Nvidia has just one class of shares. Trump on Sunday gave Huang his support, which likely reduces the chance that he is removed as CEO in the near term. “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on.” The president was asked if Huang should remain CEO of Nvidia, to which he replied: “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” With so many outstanding questions about the Huang scandal, few major analysts that cover Nvidia had weighed in on Monday morning about what it could mean for the company’s future. But those who did said it was a blemish on an otherwise sterling track record, which could spark even more investigations. “This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons,” wrote Dan Ives, of Yorkville Ives. “There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the Board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.” Chip analyst Stacy Rasgon of Bernstein Research summed up the gravity of the revelations: “NVIDIA is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS NVIDIA.”

articles.title: Nvidia shares slump amid investigation into CEO Jensen Huang
articles.summary: Huang admits infidelity, denies compromising Nvidia security as China spy inquiry shakes $4.5 trillion AI firm.
articles.body:
Nvidia stock tumbled in early trading after the company launched an internal investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation.

News of the probe into the California-based semiconductor giant sent its stock tumbling over 4 percent as United States financial markets opened for the week, while tech stocks and wider indexes rose.

The probe comes amid reports that Huang developed a close personal relationship with a Chinese business executive of a Nvidia partner company who allegedly passed information to Beijing. In a letter to employees, Huang admitted to not being faithful to his wife, but did not elaborate on the details of the relationship.

“NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” Huang said in the letter.

On Sunday, the firm announced the investigation. “The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said in a statement.

“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

The investigation puts Huang’s future in the spotlight at a company with a market capitalisation of $4.5 trillion. Huang is Nvidia’s fifth-largest shareholder, owning 3.6 percent of the company, according to LSEG data. However, Nvidia’s co-founder does not have majority voting control, unlike executives at other companies in the sector, such as Meta and SpaceX.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq was not affected by Nvidia’s downturn on Monday, with the index up 2.7 percent in early trading. Microsoft rose 2.2 percent, with chip maker AMD trading up over 10 percent on a new deal with Google and a stock analyst’s upgrade. Digital and e-commerce giant Amazon rose 3.8 percent.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1.7 percent, and the S&P 500 rose 2.1 percent.

Analysts are sceptical that the controversy surrounding Huang will lead to him stepping down.

“Founder-led companies outperform because one person carries the vision,” Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founders 100 ETF, told Al Jazeera.

“Based on the current information, I would see that as highly improbable [that he is removed].”

This is not the first investigation into Huang’s relationships in recent months. In October, The New York Times reported that the CEO had a relationship with the alleged China operative, Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed. The two Huangs are not related.

Megaspeed, a data centre and cloud computing company, described itself as “a core business partner of NVIDIA’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region” on its website.

US authorities investigated and concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, although the Chinese government pushed back against those allegations.

“The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.

The developments come amid a rough week for artificial intelligence (AI) investors on Wall Street. After markets settled following definitive results in the US midterm elections, candidates who ran on anti-AI platforms won overwhelmingly, giving Democrats, who are more critical of the AI industry than their Republican colleagues, control of both the House and the Senate in the new Congress.

Additionally, all but one of the data centre ballot measures seeking to restrict construction of new facilities across the US passed, sending shares of major AI firms tumbling on Thursday before they rose again on Friday.

“Jensen has two sets of enemies in Washington: China hawks who want the export door shut, and the crowd trying to stop the data centre buildout. The longer this drags, the stronger they get,” Monaghan told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Musk says Tesla on the hook for Cybertruck deposits after cancellation
articles.summary: Believe it or not, Tesla will have to refund some buyers a deposit placed on Cybertrucks.
articles.body:
Tesla ( TSLA ) will have to refund some buyers a deposit placed on Cybertrucks. This comes as the company was sitting on a significant amount of unsold supply only last year.

In a post made early Monday morning, CEO Elon Musk wrote, "Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people."

The news comes after Musk announced late last week that Cybertruck production would end in the middle of next year in order to focus on Cybercab - Tesla's robotaxi - production.

For many in the industry, ending Cybertruck production wasn't a surprise. Musk once boasted that Cybertruck demand was " so far off the hook, you can't even see the hook ," and the company said it had over 1 million preorders.

But conversion to sales never materialized. Cox Automotive's Kelley Blue Book estimated overall sales for the controversial pickup only hit around 71,000 since the vehicle went on sale in 2023. Tesla and Musk had built out capacity at Giga Austin to produce 250,000 Cybertrucks per year; Tesla was selling about one-tenth that amount.

The curious part is why a backlog exists for a product that seemingly didn't sell well, with unsold Cybertrucks stuffing parking lots and Tesla cutting back on shifts for the Cybertruck.

It's possible that after Tesla cut back on supply so severely over the last few months, new orders started piling up when news broke that the Cybertruck would be canceled.

Per Tesla's website, orders for either the Premium All-Wheel Drive ($92,490) or Cyberbeast ($102,490) have a delivery window of January 2027 to March 2027. It is unclear how many deposits Tesla would have to refund if it cannot meet its backlog - though each customer deposit is $1,000.

In his post today, Musk did not address Cybertruck's poor sales, but he did say the controversial truck made money. "This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media, but rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production," he said in his Monday morning post.

Cutting a product after only four years of sales - at least in the auto industry - means it was not in high demand. Betting on the Cybercab in lieu of the Cybertruck may be the right long-term call, but also gives Musk an excuse to sunset his triangle-shaped pickup.

Pras Subramanian is the lead auto reporter for Yahoo Finance. You can follow him on X and on Instagram .

articles.title: Uber launches parking service following SpotHero acquisition, with an eye on robotaxis
articles.summary: Uber Parking is the latest example of the company offering products beyond its core ride-hailing service.
articles.body:
Uber on Monday said it is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities, about nine months after the ride-hailing company acquired parking app SpotHero.

The acquisition, announced back in February, gives Uber access to a network of 13,000 garages, lots, and valet services across more than 400 cities, the company said. And while Uber's initial plans will focus on human drivers, the company also plans to leverage these parking spots to help the dozens of autonomous vehicle companies it has partnered with.

Uber said the parking spots could be used as staging and waiting locations for autonomous vehicles to help reduce congestion and deadheading, which refers to the miles a vehicle travels without a paying passenger or cargo on board.

For now, the company plans to focus on commuters driving their own vehicles. Uber said it will initially launch in 15 U.S. cities, including Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, Nashville, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, DC.

Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi indicated earlier this month that the company wants the app to be more relevant to commuters.

"Commute is one of our largest categories," he said during Uber's third-quarter earnings call. "And to be able to offer commuters an Uber to work, a pass to avoid surge, and parking if they want it when they want to drive is a great example of us building out our inventory of services to the commuter who is a top customer for us."

The parking service is the latest in a series of efforts at Uber to build an ecosystem of products that keep customers engaged with its app for everything from hailing a ride and ordering food and groceries, to packing delivery, renting cars, booking hotels , and connecting users with public transit and robotaxis.

Uber's membership program, called Uber One, is a key part of that strategy. Uber One attracts subscribers by offering rewards and credits, perks that have helped the program grow to more than 55 million members as of September 30. For instance, Uber is offering members a chance to earn 10% back in credits on eligible parking reservations. Those credits can later be used for rides and Uber Eats orders.

Uber Parking can be accessed directly on the app's homescreen. Users can enter their destination, select the date and time they need parking, and then review options on an interactive map. Users can filter the results to find self-parking, valet, garages, or surface lots. All pricing is shown upfront.
