articles.title: Celebrity chef Robert Irvine on the big mistake fast food giants are making
articles.summary: Celebrity chef Robert Irvine says fast food chains could use more humanity in their businesses as they look to jump-start sales.
articles.body:
Fast food chains could use more humanity in their businesses as they look to jump-start sales after a mostly challenging year.

"I think that the mistakes of these major companies — and there are some that are getting it right, by the way — they're trying to put profit over people, and that's the business way, right?" celebrity chef Robert Irvine said on the Power Players with Brian Sozzi podcast (video above; listen in below). "I think if you listen to the people, and we start to change habits, instead of thinking about profit … profit will come. You do the right things, profit and money will always come to you."

Sales for the fast food industry have been mixed at best this year as consumers push back on ever-rising prices.

Same-store sales across the limited-service sector rose a meager 1.6% in the first half of 2026, according to Black Box Intelligence. Guest counts fell 2% over the same period. Sales essentially increased because prices went up. Guest counts fell as prices went up.

Listen and subscribe to Power Players with Brian Sozzi on Apple Podcasts , Amazon Music , Spotify , YouTube , or wherever you find your favorite podcasts.

Quick-service restaurant menu prices are up roughly 24% to 25% since 2020 across most major brands, Black Box Intelligence pointed out.

But that has started to backfire on brands not investing aggressively in upleveling their customer service.

The largest example is McDonald's ( MCD ). After a challenging first half of the year, weakness continued into the third quarter. US same-store sales fell 0.2% on lower guest counts.

On the flip side of the coin, improvements in order speed and customer service saw Starbucks ( SBUX ) notch an impressive 7.7% US same-store sales increase in its most recent quarter.

Restaurant Brands ( QSR )-owned Burger King saw a stellar 8.4% same-store sales increase in the third quarter amid improved ingredients for its Whopper and nuggets .

Irvine is speaking from the standpoint of someone with major street cred in the food business.

Irvine launched his culinary career as a teenager by enlisting in the UK's Royal Navy, where he received rigorous foundational training in cooking aboard military vessels. He later rose to international fame as a television personality, hosting high-stakes Food Network programs such as "Restaurant: Impossible."

Beyond entertainment, Irvine has built an extensive business portfolio that spans health-focused foods, cookbooks, restaurants, and active fitness advocacy.

A devoted supporter of service members, he has partnered directly with the Pentagon and the US military to overhaul dining facilities and replace outdated mess-hall menus with high-performance nutritional programs.

articles.title: Jensen Huang is living proof that AI’s rockstar CEOs are also a hidden risk
articles.summary: Jensen Huang is not just the face of Nvidia. He’s arguably the most important person in the most critical industry on the planet.
articles.body: Jensen Huang is not just the face of Nvidia. He’s arguably the most important person in the most critical industry on the planet. Huang masterminded Nvidia’s meteoric rise into a $4.5 trillion behemoth at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom. Huang is its irreplaceable hype man, conduit to the White House and foreign capitals, and super hero who comes to the rescue by putting out fires in the AI trade on Wall Street. But the Nvidia CEO now finds himself at the center of a stunning scandal sending shockwaves across Wall Street, Washington and Silicon Valley over his admitted affair with an executive who was reportedly working with Chinese intelligence. The controversy lays bare a major but often overlooked vulnerability in the AI boom: The fortunes of many of these unthinkably powerful companies are inextricably linked to a single person. So-called “key man risk” is not just an obstacle for Nvidia: “Key man risk has never been more of a blessing and a curse,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNN in a phone interview. “We’ve always had powerful CEOs but never in history have we been at a point where such an important industry is run by people you can count on two hands.” The nature of AI – incredibly complex, secretive and specialized – makes it especially susceptible to one-person rule. “When you think about CEOs who can see around corners, they don’t grow on trees,” Ives said. ‘Solar system model’ Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the Yale professor known as the “CEO Whisperer,” said he’s fine with founders having outsized voting power, but stressed that companies “can’t surrender all control.” “These companies have created a solar system model of leadership and that can be problematic. You need to build bench strength,” said Sonnenfeld, who has studied CEO succession and whose Chief Executive Leadership Institute last year honored Huang with its Yale Legend in Leadership Award. Nvidia’s board investigation into Huang exposes a major weakness: There is no obvious bench of talent who can quickly be tapped to replace him, if needed. “There is no board succession plan, which is extraordinary. Jensen has bragged about having 60 direct reports. That’s crazy,” said Sonnenfeld. Why succession planning matters It’s a stark contrast to the leadership model at other companies that have focused intensely, with varying degrees of success, on building a bench of talented executives who could take over if a scandal, health emergency or other sudden event forces the leader out. For instance, JPMorgan Chase has built such a strong roster of experienced talent behind longtime CEO Jamie Dimon that the company regularly loses top lieutenants to rivals on Wall Street. But SpaceX recently warned investors that the company is “highly dependent” on Musk’s continued service and performance. “The loss of Mr. Musk, whether due to death, disability, or otherwise, or his inability or unwillingness to continue in his current roles,” SpaceX wrote in a filing, “could significantly disrupt our management structure, adversely affect our ability to execute our strategic plans, and negatively impact our reputation and relationships with customers, partners and other stake holders.” While Nvidia’s most recent annual financial report to regulators does not directly spell out how much the company’s fate is linked to Huang, the filing does note the company is “highly dependent” on the services of its executive team. It also acknowledges that “failure to ensure effective succession planning” could “hinder our strategic planning, execution and long-term success.” AI’s everything man Huang prides himself on being an indispensable part of Nvidia’s incredible rags-to-riches story, a tale that began at a Denny’s in 1993 and has morphed into one of the world’s most valuable companies. Time and again, Huang has emerged as the most powerful force in this turbulent industry. When AI safety fears rocked Washington, Huang was front and center as President Donald Trump explained how the industry can police itself. When worries about cheaper open models from China sparked selling in global markets, Huang teamed up with Wall Street power players to cobble together a $500 billion plan aimed at keeping the flow of money pumping into AI-powering chips. Huang has also served as the AI industry’s ambassador on the international stage. He recently met with leaders in European capitals, pitching them on the idea of sovereign AI, where every country needs to build and control its own AI systems. And Huang has presided over Nvidia’s effort to build out the AI ecosystem. In September, the company disclosed a staggering $99 billion worth of equity investments in this space, up from $2.2 billion two years ago. “Jensen is the global face of AI. You can’t replace him with one, two or three other candidates,” said Ives. “He’s not just a CEO, he’s the most powerful person in the world in the AI industry.” Huang often speaks about how he’s repeatedly saved Nvidia from near–death experiences. He even built one of the company’s internal mottos around that theme: “Our company is thirty days from going out of business.” ‘Like a James Bond movie gone horribly wrong’ That’s why the past couple of days have been such an earthquake. Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday it is investigating reports that Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair, saying he was “unfaithful” and that his actions hurt his wife and children. “I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it,” Huang said, adding that he supports Nvidia’s investigation. While Huang did not name the other person in the affair, US officials reportedly suspect that individual fed intelligence to China and helped smuggle advanced AI chips into that country. “I’ve seen everything covering tech for 30 years, but this is a shock. It’s just mind-boggling for investors,” said Ives. “It’s like a James Bond movie gone horribly wrong.” ‘If he was any other employee….’ Sonnenfeld sees only a 50/50 chance that Huang keeps his job. The Yale professor questioned how Huang will continue to simultaneously run Nvidia while facing multiple investigations from his board and various congressional committees. Sonnenfeld said it’s possible Nvidia’s board decides to elevate Huang out of direct management by giving him a symbolic role for the sake of continuity. Another option, according to Sonnenfeld, could be to bring in an experienced former tech CEO who has a deep understanding of AI, such as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. “The board could come up with alternatives to avoid being held hostage,” Sonnenfeld said. “If he was any other employee, he’d be fired. But he’s just so central. His name is bigger than Nvidia’s.”

articles.title: Anthropic debuts Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 models as IPO nears
articles.summary: Anthropic has debuted its Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 AI models.
articles.body:
Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 AI models on Monday.

The company's most powerful models, Anthropic says Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 generate outputs 30% faster than their predecessors and offer improvements across coding, reasoning, and vision.

Fable 5.2 is available across the company's platforms today. Mythos 5.2 is limited to organizations that are a part of Anthropic's Life Sciences and Cyber verification programs.

The company says Fable 5.2 will also be less expensive to run than Fable 5.1. Fable 5.2 will now cost $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million inputs and $50 per million outputs.

Tokens are a unit of measurement in AI that represent pieces of words or phrases you type or speak to a model and its responses.

AI companies are engaged in a pricing war as models become more efficient and customers look for ways to save on AI services.

Industry experts say that over time enterprises will likely rely on a mix of closed-weights models like Anthropic's and open-weights AI models to meet their needs. The idea is to avoid being locked into a single model vendor, while also being able to reduce overall costs.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 come ahead of Anthropic's anticipated initial public offering later this month.

But recent market turmoil around the AI trade could derail that.

While Wall Street was initially targeting upwards of a $2 trillion valuation for Anthropic's debut, but that could now end up between $1 trillion and $1.5 trillion.

There are also concerns that the company could end up pushing out its debut to a later date in hopes that market conditions will improve.

articles.title: Joe Rogan helped Trump win the White House. Now his show is exposing divisions inside it
articles.summary: In 2024, Joe Rogan’s podcast was a platform for President Donald Trump, helping him win reelection. This year, it’s a place for a whistleblower-style conversation alleging “corruption” at the highest levels of the Trump administration.
articles.body: In 2024, Joe Rogan’s podcast was a platform for President Donald Trump, helping him win reelection. This year, it’s a place for a whistleblower-style conversation alleging “corruption” at the highest levels of the Trump administration. That’s quite a shift — and it doesn’t bode well for Trump’s final two years in office. Last Friday, Rogan released an episode with Calley Means, the MAHA advocate and former adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who resigned in late October. Means spoke with urgency on the podcast, accusing Trump’s inner circle of blocking healthy-food policies and favoring corporate lobbyists and donors. He singled out chief of staff Susie Wiles, though he said his bigger target was the “system,” not Wiles. Wiles had already submitted her resignation by the time the episode was published, according to CNN’s reporting on Trump naming Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff. But Means certainly intended to get Wiles removed — and to call out the administration’s MAHA failures. He blamed big-money special interests for stymying progress, telling Rogan: “They’ve got the corporate money” while “we have you, we have truth getting out there. Like, and, shaming the system. Shame works. Like, the truth getting out there actually works.” Later in the episode, Means said that while working inside the government, he would often “threaten” the possibility of “bad press” to push through his and Kennedy’s agenda items. “That’s all that moves anything,” he said… “All that matters is special interest money or whether they’re going to get a bad article [written] about them.” “Oh my God,” Rogan sighed. The whole conversation seemed to weigh heavily on the host, who’d generally rather be joking with friends or speculating about Bigfoot (that was in an episode earlier in the week). And the episode underscored something about how media works in 2026: Means chose a free-flowing, hours-long podcast to speak out against the Trump administration before granting a more traditional network television interview. The Rogan episode had an immediate impact. “We’re looking at this very case,” Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, told Dana Bash on CNN’s “State of the Union.” Republican Sen. Ron Johnson also brought it up on Fox News, saying Means laid out Washington corruption “in gory detail.” Shortly after the podcast came out on Friday, Kennedy tweeted out a statement alluding to Means’ claims, albeit without naming his former adviser. “Entrenched interests have exercised power in Washington under both parties for decades,” Kennedy wrote. “President Trump and I intend to keep fighting until the American people — not corporate influence — drive our health policies. I stand firmly behind President Trump and the historic reforms we are advancing together.” The episode has also resulted in legal threats. One of Means’ targets, Trump’s top political adviser James Blair, pushed back on Means via X over the weekend, and said he’d put Means on notice that “I’d consider suing him if he defamed me.” And a spokesperson for Wiles told Axios that “Means’ accusations are outrageous, defamatory and provably false.” Even former Trump White House press secretary Sean Spicer sounded stunned. “I’ve seen a lot in 30 years,” he told The Huddle’s Dan Turrentine on Monday. “What I’ve never seen is what Calley Means did… I’ve never seen someone burn down the house like Calley Means did.” Means kept up the pressure on Monday, writing that “the Joe Rogan episode has caused cultural impact because everyone watching knows it’s true.” He suggested that others have evidence of “corporate capture” and should share it: “To current and former leaders in the admin – it is time to speak out. It is time to speak to the press about what you saw.” Means taped a follow-up interview with Margaret Brennan for Sunday’s “Face the Nation” on CBS and said that some of Trump’s senior advisors treated the president “like a baby in many respects.” When Brennan asked if Trump knew in advance that Means was going to go public on Rogan’s show, Means said, “I have no idea. I know the president is close with Joe Rogan and appreciates his opinion.” Last April, Rogan joined Trump in the Oval Office for the signing of an executive order aimed at encouraging expanded research into psychedelic drugs, a policy Rogan had personally urged the president to pursue. But Rogan’s access to Trump hasn’t stopped him from criticizing the administration on his podcast, including over ICE and the war in Iran, among other topics. Trump’s courting of podcasters like Rogan was thought to be an important part of his media campaign in 2024 – so much so that its absence during the midterm election cycle also garnered attention. Trump adviser Alex Bruesewitz was asked about it on Fox News over the weekend. “They weren’t there for us this go-around. They weren’t there to engage,” he acknowledged. Bruesewitz also suggested that some of the Republican Party’s highest-profile candidates in key races weren’t particularly appealing as podcast guests. “Somebody like a Roger Marshall, for example, wouldn’t be a compelling guest on a program like Theo Von or Joe Rogan,” he said. “So it was a much different dynamic this go-around.”
